title: Formative Checkpoints: Peer and Self-Assessment Checklists
summary: Build simple, student-friendly checklists from the official Cambridge criteria for writing, speaking, reading and listening, and teach students to use them for peer and self-assessment.

sections.h: Why students should check their own work
p: Formative assessment means checking learning while it happens, so it can still be improved. Students who learn to check their own work become independent learners. They understand what a good answer looks like. They find their own mistakes. They know what to practise next.
Cambridge speaks of learners who reflect, and teachers who build practice from reflection. A checklist is a small, simple tool for this.
Benefits:
• Students understand the marking criteria in plain words.
• Feedback arrives sooner, not weeks later.
• You mark less, because students fix many errors first.
• Students feel responsible for their progress.

b: It is not a test or a grade.
It is not a list of every grammar rule.
It is a small number of clear questions for one task.

p: Use these rules.
• Base it on the official criteria. For writing: Table A Content and Table B Language. For speaking: Grammar, Vocabulary, Development, Pronunciation.
• Use simple words and 'I' statements: 'I covered all three bullet points.'
• Keep it short: five to eight items.
• Make each item easy to answer yes or no, or with a traffic light.
• Link to action: after the check, students must fix one thing or set one target.
• Update the checklist when students are ready for the next step.
• Teach students how to use it. Use it first on a sample, not on their own work.

b: Green: I did this well.
Amber: I did this a little.
Red: I did not do this.
Choose one red or amber item to improve first.

p: Here is a checklist based on the Content table (task fulfilment and development of ideas) and the Language table (range, accuracy and organisation).
Content:
• I answered all three bullet points.
• Everything I wrote is about the task.
• I used a friendly style, like talking to a friend.
• I added reasons, details or examples.
Language:
• I used different words, not the same word again and again.
• I tried some longer sentences with 'because', 'although' or 'which'.
• I checked my verbs and tenses.
• I used linking words such as 'first', 'then', 'so' and 'but'.
• My email has a short start and a short ending.
Length:
• I wrote about 120 to 160 words.
Final step: choose one thing to improve and rewrite one sentence.

b: Do not use very formal expressions in an email to a friend.
Do not confuse 'take place' and 'take part'.
Keep the tenses clear and do not mix past and present by mistake.

sections.h: Checklist 2: Exercise 6, the report, article, review or essay
p: Content:
• I used the type of text the task asked for (report, article, review or essay).
• I used some of the ideas in the prompts and developed them.
• I added at least one idea of my own.
• I wrote for the right reader in the right style (more formal).
• I did not copy the prompts word for word.
Language:
• I used a range of vocabulary, including some less common words.
• I used a range of structures, simple and complex.
• My paragraphs are in a clear order: introduction, main points, conclusion.
• I used linking words and phrases such as 'however', 'in addition' and 'for example'.
• My conclusion uses different words from my introduction.
Length:
• 120 to 160 words.
These match what the examiner report says: balanced comments, development of ideas and cohesion help students reach the higher levels.

b: Underline the idea you added yourself.
Circle three linking words.
Count the words.

p: Based on the four marking criteria. Students can use it after a practice talk with a partner or after listening to their own recording.
Grammar:
• I used the right tense for each question (present, past, future).
• I tried a longer structure, such as 'if ...' or 'which ...'.
• I corrected myself when I noticed a mistake.
Vocabulary:
• I used words that fit the topic.
• I used at least three new words or phrases from our lessons.
• I did not repeat the same word all the time.
Development:
• I gave a reason and an example for each answer.
• I talked about both options on the card.
• I said which option I prefer and why.
• I kept speaking until the end of the two minutes.
Pronunciation:
• My words were clear.
• I stressed the important words.
• My voice went up and down to show meaning.
For the peer: say two stars (two good things) and a wish (one thing to improve next time).

b: Level 3: I give simple answers and sometimes add a reason.
Level 4: I give relevant answers and mostly add reasons and examples.
Level 5: I give developed answers with a wide range of words and structures, and I speak with ease.

p: A reading checklist helps students use good strategies.
Before reading:
• I read the title, the pictures and the questions.
• I underlined the key words in each question.
While reading:
• I looked for the paragraph that matches each question.
• I read the whole paragraph, not only one sentence.
• I looked for the same idea in different words (paraphrase).
• I watched for words like 'however', 'but' and 'although' that change the meaning.
• For multiple choice I checked each option against the text.
After reading:
• My short answers are exact. I did not add extra wrong details.
• I checked my notes are under the right heading.
• I checked my spelling of the words I copied.

b: Which question was hardest?
Why did I miss it?
What will I try next time?

p: Listening is a skill where students cannot go back, but they hear each recording twice. A checklist helps them use both listening opportunities well.
Before listening:
• I read the questions and options.
• I predicted words I might hear.
First listening:
• I got the main idea and marked an answer.
Second listening:
• I checked my answers.
• I listened for the idea, not only the same words. I know the option may use different words from the recording.
• I paid attention to the speaker's voice and opinion.
After listening:
• I looked at the script and found where each answer was.
• I wrote the words I did not catch and practised them.

ex.t: A tip from the examiner report
b: Many errors come from choosing an option because a word was heard, not because the idea matched.
Practise matching ideas, not words.

p: Do not just hand out the checklist. Teach it in four steps.
• Model: use the checklist on a sample answer on the board, and think aloud.
• Practise together: students check a second sample in pairs, then compare with the teacher.
• Use on their own work: students check a draft and tick.
• Act on it: students make one change, then hand in the improved version.
Peer feedback tips:
• Start with two good things.
• Give one clear wish. Be kind and specific.
• Use the checklist words, not 'it is bad'.
• Do not give marks, only comments.
To avoid students ticking everything, ask them to show evidence: 'Underline the three linking words'.

b: Star 1: You used 'although' correctly.
Star 2: Your introduction is friendly.
Wish: Try to add a reason in the third paragraph.

p: Use a simple tracker so students can see growth.
• Skill tracker: a table with the skill codes (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4 in your own words) and traffic lights each month.
• Targets: each student has one target for each month, for example 'use three linking words in every paragraph'.
• Portfolio: keep one piece of writing and one recorded talk each month. Compare them at the end of term.
• Review with the teacher: five minutes with each student each term to talk about the tracker.
Use the information. If most students are amber in W2, plan a lesson on linking. If most are green, move on. Share progress with students and parents in simple words.

b: Skill: Writing, organisation.
My target: use linking words.
How I will practise: check each email with the checklist.
Date to check: 30 November.

activity: Choose one skill. Build a student checklist of five to eight 'I' statements from the Cambridge criteria. Test it with a partner and a sample answer. Revise it. Then teach your students to use it with one piece of work and collect their feedback.

check.q: What is a good number of items for a student checklist?
What should students do after they use a checklist?
o: Make one change to improve their work

check.q: Which statement is student-friendly and based on the writing criteria?
o: I answered all three bullet points

title: Course Wrap-Up: Your Learning Tracker, Action Plan and Final Assessment
summary: Update your KWL chart for Week 5, review your whole course portfolio, write a 90-day action plan, learn where to find more help and prepare for the final assessment.

sections.h: Your Week 5 entry and the whole-course reflection
p: Update the L column of your KWL chart for Week 5. Write at least two specific things you learned about teaching approaches and making resources.
Then look back at your very first K column from Week 1. Write one paragraph that answers three questions:
• What do I now know that I did not know before?
• What will I do differently in my classroom?
• What do I still want to learn?
Be specific. For example: 'I used to talk for most of the lesson. Now I plan pair tasks and I check Student Talking Time every week.'

b: Learned: TBL has three stages: pre-task, task cycle and language focus.
Learned: scaffold, stretch, swap, select and supplement when adapting a textbook.
Learned: student checklists should be short and use 'I' statements.
Question: how do I run speaking tests for a class of 45?

p: You have built many useful things across five weeks. Put them into one folder, on paper or on a computer, with a clear name for each.
• Week 1: a two-year outline and notes on entries and access arrangements.
• Week 2: a marking portfolio with sample marked answers, a speaking marking sheet and notes from the examiner reports.
• Week 3: a year map with an exam buffer, a scheme of work and a diagnostic test.
• Week 4: a four-column scheme for two weeks, a lesson plan, a bank of starters and plenaries, an integrated skills sequence and a past paper sequence.
• Week 5: a TBL lesson, a speaking set, writing tasks, a reading worksheet, an adapted textbook activity and student checklists.
Look at the folder. Where are the gaps? Make a list of three things to finish.

b: Is everything saved in one place?
Is each item named and dated?
Have I shared one item with a colleague?

p: A plan keeps you moving. Choose five or six actions, each with a date.
• Days 1 to 30: use your year map and diagnostic results to set up your classes. Teach three lessons from your new lesson plan. Start a tracker.
• Days 31 to 60: run a speaking mock, a reading worksheet, a writing task, and use checklists. Meet your colleague to review results.
• Days 61 to 90: run a short mock paper, mark with the mark scheme, plan reteaching and update your scheme of work.
Make each action SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Examples:
• By 15 November: teach one TBL lesson and note STT.
• By 30 November: build two student checklists and use them.
• By 15 December: run a mock speaking day with recordings.
• By 31 January: share my best three resources with the department.

b: Action | Why | When | Help needed | Done when.

p: Keep learning. Here are good places.

• The Cambridge School Support Hub: your school's Support Coordinator can give you access. Look in the Teaching and learning section of the syllabus page for teacher guides, schemes of work, past papers, examiner reports and training information.
• The Cambridge International website: syllabus, samples database and the Cambridge Handbook.
• Cambridge professional development: online, virtual and face-to-face courses for teachers.
• Endorsed resources from publishers: check the current list.
• A colleague or mentor: observe each other and talk about lessons.
• Teacher communities in your country or online: ask for ideas and share yours.
Plan a monthly meeting with one colleague to share one lesson idea and one problem.

b: Keep a one-page 'What I tried and what happened' record.
Review it each month.
Add one new idea each time.

p: The final assessment has {{QCOUNT}} questions across all five weeks. You need 75 percent to pass and receive your certificate.
How to prepare:
• Review the key words at the top of each unit.
• Review the questions you missed in the unit practice checks.
• Review the tables: Paper 1, 2 and 3 marks and times, the Content and Language tables, the four speaking criteria.
• Review the planning ideas: year map, exam buffer, scheme of work, four columns, lesson structure, starters and plenaries.
• Review the teaching approaches: CLT, STT, TBL stages, scaffold and stretch, checklists.
In the assessment:
• Read each question and every option.
• Many questions use short classroom situations. Choose the best action.
• If you are unsure, remove options you know are wrong first.
• Check your time: take about a minute per question.

b: Teaching is a skill that grows with practice.
Small steps, repeated, make big changes.
Share what you learned with another teacher.

activity: Write your Week 5 L entries and a short paragraph that compares your Week 1 K column to what you know now. Complete your 90-day action plan with at least five actions and dates. Tell one colleague your first action.

check.q: What does SMART stand for in an action plan?
Where can teachers find Cambridge teacher guides and schemes of work?
o: The Teaching and learning section on the School Support Hub syllabus page

check.q: What is the first step in the 90-day plan?
o: Set up classes using your year map and diagnostic results
